content: The Guideline Steering Group carefully reviewed the feedback provided and incorporated it into the final document, ensuring that any conflicts of interest among members of the External Review Group were appropriately addressed. Updated recommendations were made regarding HIV prevention, infant diagnosis, antiretroviral therapy (ART) initiation, and monitoring. A simplified algorithm for diagnosing HIV in infants was also developed, particularly for lowand middle-income countries. The key principles for determining HIV infection in HIV-exposed infants and children under 18 months of age include the following: 1. 2. Conduct nucleic acid testing (NAT) for any HIV-exposed child presenting with clinical symptoms outside the national infant testing algorithm, regardless of prior NAT results. 3. At nine months of age, perform NAT for all HIV-exposed infants, whether symptomatic or asymptomatic, even if previous NAT results were negative. 4. Immediately repeat testing for any indeterminate NAT results and prioritize these cases for rapid resolution. 5. Confirm any positive NAT results with additional confirmatory testing. 6. This includes providing co-trimoxazole prophylaxis and conducting clinical and nutritional assessments. Additional notes include the following: Based on the 2016 WHO Consolidated ARV Guidelines, adding NAT at birth to the existing testing algorithm may be considered. Point-of-care (POC) NAT can be used both to diagnose HIV infection and to confirm positive results. ART should be initiated without delay, but retesting should be performed to confirm the infection. As maternal treatment coverage increases and mother-to-child transmission (MTCT) rates decrease, the likelihood of false-positive results rises. Retesting after an initial positive NAT is therefore critical to avoid unnecessary treatment, especially in settings with low transmission rates. If the second test is negative, a third NAT should be conducted before discontinuing ART. For children who were never breastfed, additional testing following a negative NAT at 4–6 weeks is included in the algorithm to account for potential false-negative results. The risk of HIV transmission persists as long as breastfeeding continues. If the nine-month test is conducted less than three months after breastfeeding cessation, infections acquired during the final days of breastfeeding may be missed. Retesting at 18 months or three months after breastfeeding cessation (whichever is later) should be performed for a final assessment of HIV status. If breastfeeding extends beyond 18 months, the final HIV diagnosis can only be made after breastfeeding ends. If breastfeeding ends before 18 months, the final diagnosis using antibody testing can only be made at 18 months. Antibody testing should be conducted at least three months after breastfeeding cessation to allow for the development of HIV antibodies. For infants under 18 months of age, NAT should be performed to confirm HIV infection.
